content:
I'm genuinely confused about Reddit and I need someone to explain it to me.

Apparently about 30% of what AI engines reference comes from Reddit. 

That makes it one of the most important surfaces for anyone who wants to be cited when people ask AI questions about their space.

Here's what I don't get. You can't promote on it, you're not supposed to talk about what you do, you're supposed to answer questions and contribute to conversations and somehow that turns into visibility over time. 

I've been watching the sales subreddits and most posts get almost no engagement at all or they post dumb questions or useless info. 

Every few months someone posts a breakdown about how Reddit drove a spike in signups or trial activations. But when you dig into the specifics, the numbers are almost always a one-time burst from a single post that hit. Not a repeatable channel with any kind of compounding logic.

Then there's the B2B question I can't stop thinking about either. Consumer products get traction on Reddit because the buyer is also the Reddit user. In B2B, the person reading the post is often not the decision maker. So even a well-received post might generate curiosity but not pipeline.  

I wrote about curiosity in my newsletter this week and how it's the skill I keep coming back to. This is one of those moments. I'm not pretending to have a framework for Reddit. I'm genuinely curious whether anyone has built it into a consistent part of their distribution strategy, not a one-off win, but something they run month over month with predictable results.

Is it a channel fit problem or an execution problem?
personaInterest: Building a consistent and predictable distribution strategy on Reddit for B2B marketing
keyTakeaway: The target persona is struggling to leverage Reddit as a scalable B2B marketing channel and is seeking advice on how to achieve predictable results.

content:
"I'm going to replace my entire 400-person SDR team with Claude Code."

A founder pitched that to Gabe Larsen a few months ago. 

Three months later the story changed. His best Claude coder turned out to be his worst sales rep, he couldn't scale any of it across the company, and there was no ROI to show for it.

I got Gabe on the Make It Happen Monday podcast this week to break this down, and it's the clearest read I've heard on where AI in sales actually is right now.

Here's the trap everyone's walking into. They watch what one person can do with AI on a laptop, see something genuinely impressive, and decide they'll build the same thing internally to replace the team. Then they find out they don't have the people or the process to make it work at scale. 

The tools pile up, the workflow gets more complicated instead of simpler, and everyone is "saving time" while nobody can point to a real result. 

Gabe calls it pretend productivity and it is everywhere.

It doesn't stop with them. If you sell into these companies, you're selling into that mess. Half your buyers think they'll build their way out of needing you, and the other half are buried in tools they can't operationalize.

AI scales beautifully for one person and falls apart the moment you push it across a team without rebuilding how that team works. That is the real replace or rebuild question, and most companies are answering it backwards.

If you're running a sales team in 2026, are you trying to build or buy your way through AI, and is it actually working yet?
personaInterest: Effectively integrating AI into sales teams and avoiding 'pretend productivity'
keyTakeaway: Many companies struggle to scale AI solutions across their sales teams, creating an opportunity for sales representatives to offer operationalized solutions that drive real results.

content:
"why did you want to talk with me instead of AI?"

I posted this a few months ago as a question I think we should start asking our prospects on an initial discovery call.  It got some pushback, with someone going as far as to call me insecure because I was asking that question.

Maybe it was insecurity but it was based on my/our new reality in this world of AI in Sales. 

I had just made the switch from ChatGPT to Claude CoWork and spent an entire weekend doing a deep dive on my business strategy, working through a laundry list of tasks and to-do's that I had been putting off for years, building apps and workflows and much more. 

After getting through everything I ended up cancelling a few contracts with vendors who had taken 6 months to complete what I just did over the weekend with AI while I cleaned my basement. 

I was super excited about what I had done and what I could do but then I got very concerned when I came to the realization that I may never talk to a sales rep again.  

Claude helped me build and now helps me run my strategy for my business. If I need something it's probably going to suggest it to me and if not, when I ask it about a service or solution I think I need, it will help me determine if I need it and then help me research the top vendors and do most of the research before I ever need to talk to a rep.  

If/when I do need to talk to a rep for whatever reason, if that rep doesn't add value immediately or tries to bring me back through their sales process I'll end the conversation faster than it started. 

I've said it for a while now that I'm not concerned with all these AI sales tools replacing sales reps. I'm concerned when the client wakes up and comes to the same realization I did - they don't us.

Or do they?

Well, I came across some data from Gartner recently that made me feel better.  

The bad new first - the % of B2B buyers who don't want to talk to a sales rep has increased from 43% to 67%. 

The good news - 69% of buyers turn to sales reps to validate AI-generated insights.

This means there is still a huge trust issue with AI and great sales reps are the answer. 

I still think average sales reps are in serious trouble and the easy way to prove this is to go into any AI platform and pretend like you're a prospect and go through the "discovery" process for your solution. If the AI can answer any question as good or better than you then you're in trouble. 

However, if you go through that process and find errors or a lack of important details or context then you're going to be even more valuable moving forward. 

Maybe we shouldn't phrase the question as "why did you want to talk with me instead of AI?" but instead ask "what have you learned from AI so far and what additional questions do you have or information do you need to validate to help you make a decision?"

Let me know what you think in the comments.
personaInterest: Understanding the role of AI in sales and how to validate AI-generated insights
keyTakeaway: Buyers are increasingly relying on AI for research, but still require sales reps to validate AI-generated insights, creating an opportunity for reps to add value and build trust.

Who remembers Drakkar Noir?

I walked into a local store recently and a woman had a table set up with homemade candles on it. 

She was greeting everyone who walked with a huge smile and big "HELLO! I hope you're having a great day today. If you are, I have a candle with sunshine written all over it to keep the good vibes going. If you're not, I have one that will brighten your day or help you relax!"

I was drawn to her energy and positivity and promised I would stop by on my way out. 

When I stopped back at her table on the way out she told me her story of how one day she decided to bet on herself and follow her passion by starting a candle business.  She made every one of them by hand and came up with fun fragrances and names for every candle. 

I asked her if she was happy that she made the leap and how she was doing?

She said that it was definitely not the best way to make a living but she was happier now than she ever had been in corporate because she gets to put smiles on people's faces every day.

I love supporting local businesses and I love supporting people who take a chance on themselves even more so I bought 10 candles. 

My favorite one is highlighted below. IYKTK 😜

#80skid #GenXer4life
personaInterest: Supporting local businesses and entrepreneurs who take risks to pursue their passions
keyTakeaway: Decision-makers who have taken a leap of faith to start their own business may be more open to innovative solutions that support their unique needs and values.

content:
Curiosity is not a soft skill. It's THE skill.

I had Ishan Shabanad on the Make It Happen Monday Podcast this week and he said something that "hit hard" (iykyk 😉): "Remain curious about your own potential. If you were presented something and it didn't bear fruit, that doesn't mean your journey stops."

He spent the first 20 years of his life in a monastery where he trained in ancient yogic traditions, martial arts, and breath work. He then left the monastery, got a DBA from Swiss School of Business Management in Geneva, became a research fellow at Stanford, and now works with veterans, healthcare workers, and elite performers on resilience and human potential. 🤯.  

He has lived two completely different lives and the thing that connected both of them was curiosity.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately. I wrote a post about it last week and highlighted it in my newsletter after the same theme kept showing up in conversation after conversation. 

As I outlined in my newsletter, I got curious about curiosity and used AI to learn about George Loewenstein's information gap theory from Carnegie Mellon.  I found a UC Davis study that showed curious people don't retain more about the thing they're curious about, they retain more about EVERYTHING happening around them. It's called the "vortex effect."

This all connects to Sales because that's what great sellers do. They catch the throwaway comment about a leadership change. They notice the hesitation when a prospect mentions their current vendor. They pick up on the stalled initiative from last quarter that nobody else asked about. 

Those details are where deals live. And they only show up when you're genuinely curious.

Ultimately, I think genuine, across-the-board curiosity is something you're born with. But you can teach people to be curious about specific things. The key is interest. If you can get someone interested in a topic, a company, a person, curiosity follows on its own. Interest is the on-ramp.

In a world where AI can give you any information you need at the drop of a dime, the people who win are the ones curious enough to look for it, validate it, and explore it without looking for the answer.

That's the difference between using AI as a crutch and using it as a force multiplier.

What keeps you curious?
personaInterest: The power of curiosity in driving success, particularly in sales and leveraging AI as a tool for growth
keyTakeaway: Sales representatives can leverage genuine curiosity to uncover hidden deal opportunities by paying attention to subtle details and using AI as a force multiplier to explore and validate information.

content:
"What's the best tip/trick you have for getting through AI gatekeepers?"

I've gotten that question (or variation of) multiple times in the past few weeks so I thought I'd do a post about it and see what others think. 

First off, "tricks" don't work for AI call screeners just like they don't work for live call screeners.  

There's no magical thing you can say that's going to make an AI agent let you through.  

Remember, AI isn't the actual screener, the person who is listening to your message and/or wrote the screening rules is.

Also, any call screener's job isn't to block you 100%.  It's to SCREEN your call and only let through the ones that are relevant. 

Think about it for a second, if there's a VP of Sales on the other end of the call who is missing quota, has an empty pipeline and their reps are demotivated because they don't feel like they're being invested in, is that call screener doing their job by not letting me (JB Sales Training) through?  No, they aren't.  However, I'm also not doing my job by giving them a good enough reason to let me through. 

With that, I have the same advice for both live and AI screeners - have a relevant and personalized REASON for your call based on research (i.e. trigger event). 

Here's what gets screened out every time:
❌ "Hi, this is Sarah from XYZCompany. I'd like to talk to David about our platform."

There's no context, relevance or reason.

Now here are a few examples of what it sounds like with a 'reason' based on 30 seconds of research: 
✅"I'm calling because I saw your Q2 numbers came in a little light. I wanted to talk to David about what's working for other sales leaders rebuilding pipeline right now."
✅"I'm calling because I saw you have 15 open sales roles posted. I wanted to talk to David about how other teams are onboarding that many new reps without it falling apart."
✅"I'm calling because I noticed your team rolled out Gong recently. I wanted to talk to Sarah about what separates the teams where those tools actually work from the ones where they don't."
✅"I'm calling because I saw the restructuring announcement last month. I wanted to connect with David about how other leaders are deciding whether to retrain the team they kept or bring in new people."

Every one of those is under 15 seconds and focuses on earning the next 30 seconds of conversation. Remember, during a cold call you're job isn't to sell your solution, it's to sell the next step. With a call screener, you're trying to pique their interest enough to earn a conversation. 

AI gatekeepers aren't a new obstacle. They're forcing a discipline the best reps already had. If you can't articulate why you're calling before you pick up the phone, you're not ready to dial.

What are you seeing work to get through these AI screeners? Genuinely curious whether anyone has found a consistent approach beyond having a relevant reason for the call.
personaInterest: Overcoming obstacles in sales outreach and improving cold calling effectiveness
keyTakeaway: Personalized and relevant reasons for calls, based on research and trigger events, are crucial for getting past AI gatekeepers and earning conversations with decision-makers.

content:
I haven't logged into Apollo.io in over a month.

Not because I stopped using it. Because Apollo's MCP connector lets me run everything through Claude now.

Here's what that actually looks like.

I set up three outbound sequences in Apollo for three completely different audiences. Former Salesforce people I've trained who now lead sales teams at new companies. Manufacturing and industrial companies outside the SaaS world. And dormant customers I've worked with over the past few years. 

Apollo handles the identification, enrichment, sequencing, and execution for all three.

Last week I asked Claude to pull the analytics on my Tier 2 manufacturing sequence. Within seconds it went into Apollo, grabbed the open rates, reply rates, and engagement data, and came back with specific insights on what messaging was landing and what wasn't.

I then told Claude we needed to update the messaging based on what the data was showing. It went back into Apollo, rewrote the sequence copy, and created a separate Tier 2 sequence so we could start testing the new version against the original. 

I didn't open Apollo once. I didn't toggle between tabs. I didn't export a CSV and analyze it in a spreadsheet. The entire loop from analytics to insight to action happened in one conversation.

Now I get a daily recap of open rates, response rates, and what's working across all three tracks. All through Claude. Not Apollo.

This is what people mean when they say AI changes how you sell. It's not about automating the work. It's about compressing the feedback loop. 

What used to take me a full morning of pulling reports, reading data, rewriting emails, and rebuilding sequences now happens in a conversation. And I still approve every message before it goes out.

The tools that win aren't the ones with the most features. They're the ones that show up where you already work and let you act on data without breaking your flow. Apollo figured that out.

Link in the comments.

#ApolloPartner #ApolloAnywhere #MakeItHappen
personaInterest: Streamlining sales processes and leveraging AI to compress the feedback loop
keyTakeaway: Apollo's integration with AI tools like Claude enables seamless sales process automation, allowing reps to focus on high-value tasks and make data-driven decisions in real-time.
